questions.scenario: A fintech platform needs an assistant that, given a natural-language request like 'show me my last three transactions and the running total', decides which internal APIs to call, in what order, and how to aggregate the results.
questions.stem: Which AWS service combination MOST naturally fits this pattern?

options.text: AWS Step Functions Standard with a state machine for every supported request type.
options.why: Step Functions is deterministic orchestration. The LLM must DECIDE the steps at runtime — Step Functions cannot do that decision.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents with action groups backed by Lambda functions.
options.why: Agents let the FM reason which tool/action to call next via a ReAct loop. Action groups expose APIs to the FM; Lambda implements them.

options.text: API Gateway + Lambda + Bedrock InvokeModel with prompt templates.
options.why: Works for single-shot calls; lacks the orchestration loop, tool selection, and session memory Agents give you.

options.text: Amazon Kendra with intent classification.
options.why: Kendra is enterprise search, not multi-step tool orchestration.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agents = FM-driven multi-step orchestration with tool use. Use when the LLM must DECIDE which tool to call. Step Functions for deterministic workflows.
questions.trap_alert: If the stem says 'LLM picks which tool/API to call next', it's Agents — not Step Functions.

questions.scenario: A team is configuring a Bedrock Agent action group. They have a small set of internal functions, no existing OpenAPI spec, and they want the simplest definition.
questions.stem: Which action group definition style is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Provide an OpenAPI 3.0 schema describing each operation.
options.why: Valid option, but introducing OpenAPI maintenance overhead is unnecessary when only a few simple functions are needed.

options.text: Use the Function Detail definition style (function name + parameters defined inline).
options.why: Function Detail is the simpler alternative: just define function name, description, and parameter shapes — no OpenAPI document required.

options.text: Define everything in the agent's system prompt.
options.why: System prompt is for the agent persona/instructions, not for defining callable tools.

options.text: Skip action groups and rely on the agent's built-in tool library.
options.why: Agents don't have a generic 'built-in tool library' — actions are defined via action groups.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent action group can be defined two ways: OpenAPI 3.0 schema (richer) or Function Detail (simpler — name + parameters inline).
questions.trap_alert: Don't default to OpenAPI for everything. For a handful of simple functions, Function Detail is the documented simpler path.

questions.scenario: An enterprise wants a Bedrock Agent to invoke internal APIs that already exist behind a tightly controlled gateway in a private VPC. The team prefers to keep the API invocation logic inside their existing application rather than in a Lambda function attached to the Agent.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock Agent feature MOST appropriately supports this?

options.text: Return Control (RoC) — Agent returns the tool call details to the calling application, which executes it and returns the result.
options.why: RoC is exactly designed for this: the Agent does the reasoning, but the application code (not a Lambda action group) executes the tool call.

options.text: VPC interface endpoints for bedrock-agent-runtime.
options.why: Provides private connectivity, but does not change which code executes the tool — that's an RoC concern.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput for the Agent.
options.why: Throughput capacity has nothing to do with where the action executes.

options.text: Bedrock Flows.
options.why: Flows are a separate visual orchestration product — not the Agent action-execution model.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent action execution options: (1) Lambda function attached to the action group, OR (2) Return Control (RoC) where the application receives the tool call and executes it.
questions.trap_alert: Return Control is easy to miss. It's the right choice when 'execution must happen in the existing app, not a Lambda'.

questions.scenario: A data team finds that Claude is making arithmetic mistakes on multi-step word problems when answering tersely.
questions.stem: Which prompt-engineering technique MOST cost-effectively improves accuracy?

options.text: Few-shot prompting with three solved examples plus a Chain-of-Thought instruction ('think step by step').
options.why: CoT + few-shot examples is the canonical pattern for boosting multi-step reasoning accuracy without model changes.

options.text: Fine-tune Claude on a math dataset.
options.why: Expensive and slow vs. a prompting change that often closes the gap.

options.text: Switch to a code-generation model like Code Llama.
options.why: Code Llama is for code synthesis, not arithmetic word problems.

options.text: Set temperature to 1.0 to explore more answers.
options.why: Higher temperature INCREASES variability, not accuracy.

questions.knowledge_point: Chain-of-Thought prompting + few-shot exemplars is the cheapest first lever for reasoning accuracy. Fine-tuning is heavier and slower.
questions.trap_alert: Higher temperature = more creative, NOT more accurate. Lower temperature for deterministic answers.

questions.scenario: A workflow needs Claude to ALWAYS return a JSON object with fields `intent`, `confidence`, and `entities`. Currently the response sometimes includes a preamble like 'Sure, here is the JSON:'.
questions.stem: Which prompt technique MOST reliably enforces a clean JSON-only response?

options.text: Use a system prompt that defines the exact JSON schema AND prime the assistant turn with an opening `{` to force JSON output.
options.why: Schema-in-system + priming the response with `{` (assistant turn) is the documented Anthropic pattern for clean structured output.

options.text: Set temperature to 0.7 for creativity.
options.why: Higher creativity reduces structural compliance.

options.text: Increase max_tokens to 4096.
options.why: Length cap is unrelated to format compliance.

options.text: Ask politely 'please return JSON only'.
options.why: Less reliable than schema + priming.

questions.knowledge_point: Structured-output pattern on Claude: schema in system prompt + prime the assistant turn with the opening structural token (`{` or `[`) for clean JSON without preamble.
questions.trap_alert: Claude doesn't have a strict 'JSON mode' parameter like some providers; the priming pattern is the AWS-recommended approach.

questions.scenario: A team manages dozens of production prompts with frequent revisions. They want to safely roll forward and roll back prompt versions without redeploying the application.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock feature is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Bedrock Prompt Management — define prompts as managed resources with draft and published versions, called by ID.
options.why: Prompt Management provides versioning, variables, and IDs that can be rolled forward/back without code deploys.

options.text: Store prompts in S3 and load them at app startup.
options.why: Workable, but no native version aliasing, variables, or built-in rollback compared to Prompt Management.

options.text: Hardcode prompts in Lambda code and use Lambda versions/aliases.
options.why: Couples prompt life cycle to Lambda deploys. Higher operational overhead.

options.text: Use Bedrock Flows.
options.why: Flows compose pipelines; Prompt Management is the dedicated prompt-as-resource feature.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Prompt Management = prompts as managed resources with versions and variables. Call by ID; ship without code deploys.
questions.trap_alert: Flows orchestrates. Prompt Management VERSIONS. Don't conflate.

questions.scenario: A non-engineering team must compose a multi-step GenAI workflow with conditional branching, a KB retrieval, an FM invocation, and a Lambda data lookup — without writing orchestration code.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock feature is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Bedrock Flows — visual nodes for Prompt, Knowledge Base, Agent, Lambda, Condition, Iterator.
options.why: Flows is the visual, low-code orchestration product for multi-step GenAI pipelines with branching.

options.text: AWS Step Functions visual editor.
options.why: General orchestration, not GenAI-native; you'd manually wire FM/KB invocations.

options.text: AWS App Composer.
options.why: App Composer is for IaC composition (SAM/CDK), not runtime GenAI orchestration.

options.text: Bedrock Prompt Management.
options.why: Prompt Management stores and versions prompts; it does not orchestrate multi-step flows.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Flows: visual GenAI orchestration with nodes for Prompt, KB, Agent, Lambda, Condition, Iterator. Low-code path for multi-step pipelines.
questions.trap_alert: Flows ≠ Step Functions. Flows is GenAI-native and lower-code for prompt/KB/agent composition.

questions.scenario: A new Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet release on Bedrock requires invocation through a cross-region inference profile because on-demand single-region capacity for the model is unavailable.
questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about the request?

options.text: The InvokeModel call must reference the inference profile ARN (not the bare model ID), and traffic may be routed to one of several configured regions.
options.why: Cross-region inference profiles are referenced by ARN; the service routes the call across pre-defined regions for capacity/resilience.

options.text: The caller must explicitly choose a region for each request.
options.why: The inference profile abstracts the routing; the caller does not choose the executing region per request.

options.text: Cross-region inference replicates the model weights to your account's S3 bucket.
options.why: It does not replicate weights to the customer; AWS routes invocations.

options.text: Inference profiles only support custom imported models, not first-party FMs.
options.why: Inference profiles are explicitly supported for first-party FMs requiring cross-region capacity.

questions.knowledge_point: Cross-region inference profile: call by profile ARN; the service routes the invocation to one of the configured regions. Required for some newer model invocations.
questions.trap_alert: Quotas for cross-region inference are counted at the HOME region of the profile, not aggregated freely.

questions.scenario: A chat UI needs to render tokens as the FM produces them, to reduce perceived latency.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock API call is REQUIRED?

options.text: InvokeModel.
options.why: Returns the full response in one shot — no token streaming.

options.text: InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
options.why: Returns a stream of response chunks suitable for incremental UI rendering.

options.text: BatchInferenceJob.
options.why: Asynchronous offline batch, not interactive streaming.

options.text: InvokeAgent with streaming flag.
options.why: InvokeAgent has streaming capability but the canonical API for streaming raw model responses is InvokeModelWithResponseStream.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock streaming API = InvokeModelWithResponseStream. For Agents, InvokeAgent streams events; the question's signal is 'token-by-token chat UI'.
questions.trap_alert: InvokeModel ≠ InvokeModelWithResponseStream. The streaming variant is a separate API.

questions.scenario: An app must analyze user-uploaded product photographs to extract structured attributes (color, size, brand) into JSON.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock model family is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet (vision-capable).
options.why: Claude 3 family includes vision: send the image with a structured-output prompt to extract attributes into JSON.

options.text: Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2.
options.why: Text embeddings — cannot analyze image content.

options.text: Stability AI SDXL.
options.why: Image GENERATION, not image understanding.

options.text: Amazon Polly.
options.why: Text-to-speech.

questions.knowledge_point: Vision-capable FMs on Bedrock include Claude 3 family and Amazon Nova Lite/Pro/Premier. Use them for IMAGE UNDERSTANDING tasks; SDXL/Titan Image/Nova Canvas are GENERATION.
questions.trap_alert: Embedding models ≠ understanding models. Embeddings represent; vision models reason about content.

questions.scenario: A customer assistant Bedrock Agent must remember the user's preferences across consecutive turns within a single conversation, but state must NOT persist after the user ends the session.
questions.stem: Which capability satisfies this?

options.text: Bedrock Agent sessions identified by sessionId — the orchestrator retains conversation state until the session ends or times out.
options.why: sessionId in InvokeAgent ties multiple turns into one conversation with retained state; ephemeral by design.

options.text: Persist conversation history in DynamoDB and re-send on each call.
options.why: Works but adds custom code and persistence vs. the native session abstraction.

options.text: Enable Bedrock Memory feature with a Knowledge Base.
options.why: KBs are for grounding documents, not short-lived per-session conversational memory.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput keeps state in the model.
options.why: Throughput is capacity, not state.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent sessions: pass a consistent sessionId across InvokeAgent calls to retain conversation state in a single ephemeral session.
questions.trap_alert: Don't roll a custom DynamoDB state store when the agent's native session abstraction suffices.

questions.scenario: A platform must support a 'supervisor' AI that delegates research tasks to specialist sub-agents (one for finance, one for legal) and aggregates their findings.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock capability MOST directly supports this pattern?

options.text: Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration — supervisor agent routes tasks to sub-agents and aggregates results.
options.why: Multi-Agent Collaboration is the native pattern for supervisor + specialist agents on Bedrock.

options.text: Create a single agent with many action groups.
options.why: Possible but doesn't model true delegation between distinct agents; loses isolation benefits.

options.text: Use Step Functions to call independent Agents.
options.why: Works as deterministic orchestration; loses the FM-driven delegation choice the question implies.

options.text: Use Bedrock Flows nodes only.
options.why: Flows can orchestrate but not natively model supervisor-subagent collaboration.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Multi-Agent Collaboration: supervisor agent + specialist sub-agents, with native delegation, routing, and result aggregation.
questions.trap_alert: When the stem says 'supervisor + specialists' or 'agent of agents', the answer is Multi-Agent Collaboration.

questions.scenario: A Bedrock Agent action group is backed by a Lambda function. The team needs the action to be both secure and auditable.
questions.stem: Which configurations are REQUIRED? (Select TWO)

options.text: The Lambda's resource-based policy must grant bedrock.amazonaws.com permission to invoke it, scoped to the Agent ARN.
options.why: Bedrock invokes the Lambda on the customer's behalf; a resource-based policy with bedrock principal is required.

options.text: CloudTrail must be enabled in the region.
options.why: CloudTrail captures the InvokeAgent / Lambda invocation control-plane events — required for audit.

options.text: The Lambda must be deployed in eu-west-1 only.
options.why: No such region restriction; Lambda must be in the SAME region as the Agent runtime but the choice of region is yours.

options.text: Encrypt the Lambda code with a customer-managed KMS key.
options.why: Code encryption is optional, not REQUIRED for the integration.

options.text: Disable VPC integration on the Lambda.
options.why: VPC integration is supported and is often desired for private access.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent → Lambda action: Lambda resource-based policy grants bedrock.amazonaws.com Invoke permission; CloudTrail captures the integration audit.
questions.trap_alert: Forgetting the Lambda resource policy is the #1 cause of Agent action failures with 'access denied' errors.

questions.scenario: An entity-extraction prompt with no examples produces inconsistent output formats.
questions.stem: Which prompt technique BEST stabilizes the format?

options.text: Zero-shot with longer instructions.
options.why: More words can help, but pattern-matching against examples is stronger.

options.text: Few-shot prompting with 3–5 worked input/output examples in the user prompt.
options.why: Few-shot examples are the most reliable lever for format consistency without fine-tuning.

options.text: Increase temperature to 1.0.
options.why: Increases variability.

options.text: Use chain-of-thought.
options.why: CoT improves reasoning, not strict format compliance — sometimes makes formats noisier.

questions.knowledge_point: Few-shot examples = strongest prompting lever for format consistency. CoT = strongest for reasoning accuracy.
questions.trap_alert: CoT and few-shot solve different problems. Match the technique to the failure mode.

questions.scenario: A marketing team needs to generate product hero images programmatically in batch jobs. Cost matters; latency does not.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock model is MOST cost-effective for this batch image generation?

options.text: Amazon Titan Image Generator (with Bedrock Batch Inference).
options.why: Titan Image is purpose-built on Bedrock; combined with Batch Inference gives a ~50% cost discount for async generation.

options.text: Amazon Polly.
options.why: Polly is text-to-speech, not image generation.

options.text: Amazon Rekognition.
options.why: Rekognition is image ANALYSIS, not generation.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend.
options.why: Comprehend is NLP entity/sentiment extraction.

questions.knowledge_point: Image generation on Bedrock: Titan Image Generator, Stability AI SDXL, Amazon Nova Canvas. Batch Inference saves ~50% for async workloads.
questions.trap_alert: Rekognition is for analysis. Polly is TTS. Comprehend is NLP. Don't confuse the AI-services family with the GenAI-on-Bedrock family.

questions.scenario: A web chat app needs an architecture where browser clients stream tokens from a Bedrock model in real time via a persistent connection.
questions.stem: Which architecture is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Browser → API Gateway WebSocket → Lambda (streaming response) → Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
options.why: WebSocket gives the persistent bidirectional connection; Lambda streaming returns chunks; Bedrock streaming yields tokens incrementally.

options.text: Browser → API Gateway REST → Lambda → Bedrock InvokeModel.
options.why: REST is request/response — no streaming.

options.text: Browser → CloudFront → S3 → Bedrock.
options.why: CloudFront/S3 cannot proxy to Bedrock with streaming semantics.

options.text: Browser → SQS → Lambda → Bedrock.
options.why: SQS is async messaging, not low-latency streaming.

questions.knowledge_point: Streaming GenAI to browsers: WebSocket (API Gateway) + Lambda streaming responses + InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Or use API Gateway HTTP API with response streaming.
questions.trap_alert: REST + InvokeModel is the WRONG pattern when the requirement is token-by-token streaming.

questions.scenario: An application calls Bedrock InvokeModel directly (not via an Agent) and wants the model to decide whether to call an external 'get_weather' function based on the user's question.
questions.stem: Which Anthropic Claude feature on Bedrock MOST directly supports this?

options.text: Anthropic Claude Tool Use (Function Calling) — pass tool definitions in the Messages API; model returns a tool_use block when it decides to call.
options.why: Claude's Tool Use lets the model emit a structured tool_use block; the application executes the tool and returns a tool_result. Native pattern without Agents.

options.text: Configure a Bedrock Guardrail with an allow-list.
options.why: Guardrails are CONTENT policies, not tool-routing.

options.text: Switch to Amazon Titan and use Code Interpreter.
options.why: Titan does not expose a 'Code Interpreter' on Bedrock; not applicable.

options.text: Use Knowledge Bases to retrieve weather.
options.why: KBs retrieve static documents, not live external function calls.

questions.knowledge_point: Tool use / function calling on Bedrock via Claude Messages API: pass `tools` definitions; model returns tool_use; app executes; returns tool_result; model continues. Works without a Bedrock Agent.
questions.trap_alert: You can do tool use WITHOUT an Agent. Agents add orchestration loops + native KB integration; raw tool use is enough for simple single-call patterns.

questions.scenario: A summarization workflow must produce the SAME response for the same input across runs as much as possible.
questions.stem: Which parameter setting BEST achieves this?

options.text: temperature = 0 (or very small), top_p = 1.
options.why: Lowest temperature + maximal top_p yields the most deterministic outputs supported by the model.

options.text: temperature = 1.0, top_p = 0.9.
options.why: High temperature increases randomness.

options.text: temperature = 0.7, top_k = 250.
options.why: Mid-temperature is creative/varied.

options.text: Set max_tokens = 4000.
options.why: Length cap does not control determinism.

questions.knowledge_point: For deterministic output: temperature ≈ 0, top_p ≈ 1. Note: even at temperature 0, exact reproducibility is not always guaranteed by all model providers.
questions.trap_alert: Higher temperature = more creative, NOT more accurate. Pair with low top_p for the most deterministic decoding.

questions.scenario: A Bedrock Flow must route requests: technical questions go to a specialist KB; billing questions go to a Lambda that queries the billing system; everything else goes to a general FM prompt.
questions.stem: Which Flow node enables this routing?

options.text: Condition node — evaluates an expression and routes to one of multiple branches.
options.why: Condition is the native branching node in Bedrock Flows for if/elseif/else routing.

options.text: Iterator node.
options.why: Iterator loops over collections; it does not branch on a condition.

options.text: Lambda node only.
options.why: Lambda nodes execute custom code, but routing is the Condition node's job.

options.text: Prompt node.
options.why: Prompt nodes invoke an FM; they don't branch.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Flow node types include Input/Output, Prompt, Knowledge Base, Agent, Lambda, Condition, Iterator. Pick by purpose.
questions.trap_alert: Don't add a Lambda for what a Condition node already does — over-engineering.

questions.scenario: A team wants to customize the system prompt that a Bedrock Agent uses for pre-processing user input, orchestration reasoning, and KB summarization.
questions.stem: How is this customized?

options.text: Override the four built-in Agent prompt templates (Pre-Processing, Orchestration, KB Response Generation, Post-Processing) in the Agent configuration.
options.why: Bedrock Agents expose four overridable prompt templates per stage; each can be customized.

options.text: Send the system prompt as the first user message.
options.why: Agents have separate templates; user messages do not replace them.

options.text: Modify the underlying model weights.
options.why: Weight modification is fine-tuning, not prompt customization.

options.text: Use Bedrock Prompt Management — Agents do not have built-in templates.
options.why: Agents DO have built-in templates; this is false.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent customizable prompt templates: Pre-Processing, Orchestration, Knowledge Base Response Generation, Post-Processing.
questions.trap_alert: Customize the templates in the AGENT, not via Prompt Management. Two different features.

questions.scenario: An engineering org wants AI-assisted code generation directly inside developers' IDEs (VS Code, IntelliJ) with awareness of internal repos.
questions.stem: Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer.
options.why: Q Developer is the AWS-native code-assist tool integrated into IDEs, with code suggestions, scans, and inline chat.

options.text: Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer only.
options.why: CodeGuru reviews and suggests improvements, but isn't a real-time IDE code assistant in the same way as Q Developer.

options.text: Amazon Lex.
options.why: Lex is for chatbot intent recognition, not coding.

options.text: Amazon Polly.
options.why: Text-to-speech.

questions.knowledge_point: Amazon Q Developer = AWS's developer-focused AI assistant: IDE inline suggestions, code scans, security reviews, /transform refactoring.
questions.trap_alert: Q Developer (developer assistant) ≠ Q Business (enterprise knowledge assistant). Read the use case.

questions.scenario: A team must classify 50,000 customer reviews overnight. Latency per item does not matter; minimizing cost is critical.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock pattern is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Bedrock Batch Inference — submit a single JSONL job to S3, receive results in S3, ~50% cost saving versus on-demand.
options.why: Batch Inference is purpose-built for high-volume async inference at 50% lower per-token cost.

options.text: InvokeModel from a Lambda fan-out.
options.why: Works but more expensive (full per-token rate) and adds Lambda invocation costs.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput.
options.why: Provisioned is a 1mo/6mo commit. Overkill for a one-night job.

options.text: Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
options.why: KBs are for RAG retrieval, not bulk classification.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Batch Inference: async, S3 in/out, JSONL format, up to 24h SLA, ~50% discount vs on-demand. Designed for offline high-volume jobs.
questions.trap_alert: If the question says 'cost matters' AND 'overnight'/'async', Batch Inference is the signal — not Provisioned Throughput.

questions.scenario: A Bedrock Agent must enforce a no-PII-leakage policy on both user inputs and FM outputs.
questions.stem: Where is the Guardrail applied?

options.text: Attach the Guardrail to the Agent in its configuration — Guardrail evaluates both input and output during every Agent turn.
options.why: Bedrock Agents support a guardrailConfiguration that evaluates each turn's input and output automatically.

options.text: Wrap every Agent call in an ApplyGuardrail API call manually.
options.why: Possible, but native attachment is the cleaner managed path.

options.text: Add the Guardrail to the underlying Knowledge Base only.
options.why: KB-attached guardrails apply to retrievals; user input + FM output policing happens at the Agent level.

options.text: Guardrails cannot be used with Agents.
options.why: False — Guardrails fully integrate with Agents.

questions.knowledge_point: Guardrails can attach natively to Models, Agents, KBs — or be applied independently via the ApplyGuardrail API. Native attachment is the simplest path.
questions.trap_alert: Attach the Guardrail at the highest enclosing layer (Agent) so it covers all turns, instead of at every sub-component.

questions.scenario: A creative team wants AWS-native services for (a) generating product images from text and (b) generating short video clips from text.
questions.stem: Which combination of Bedrock models? (Select TWO)

options.text: Amazon Nova Canvas for images.
options.why: Nova Canvas is Amazon's text-to-image model on Bedrock.

options.text: Amazon Nova Reel for video.
options.why: Nova Reel is Amazon's text-to-video model on Bedrock.

options.text: Amazon Polly for video.
options.why: Polly is text-to-speech.

options.text: Anthropic Claude 3 Opus for images.
options.why: Claude vision can ANALYZE images but does not GENERATE them.

options.text: Amazon Rekognition Video for video generation.
options.why: Rekognition is video ANALYSIS, not generation.

questions.knowledge_point: Amazon Nova generation models: Nova Canvas (image), Nova Reel (video). Other image gen models on Bedrock: Titan Image Generator, Stability AI SDXL.
questions.trap_alert: Rekognition / Polly are AWS AI services that look adjacent but aren't generation models on Bedrock.

questions.stem: Which option correctly orders the runtime steps of a single InvokeAgent call where the Agent uses BOTH an attached Knowledge Base AND an action group?

options.text: Pre-processing → Orchestration (reason) → KB retrieval / Action group invocation → Post-processing → Response.
options.why: Agent runtime: pre-processing of user input, orchestration step (FM reasons), tool/KB calls as decided, post-processing for the final response.

options.text: Post-processing → Orchestration → KB retrieval → Response → Pre-processing.
options.why: Wrong order; pre-processing is first, post-processing is last.

options.text: Action group → KB retrieval → Pre-processing → Orchestration → Response.
options.why: Pre-processing comes before orchestration.

options.text: KB retrieval → Pre-processing → Action group → Orchestration → Response.
options.why: Pre-processing must precede any reasoning or tool calls.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Agent runtime stages: Pre-processing → Orchestration (reasoning loop, with KB/Action calls) → Post-processing → Response. Each stage has an overridable prompt template.
questions.trap_alert: Memorizing the four stage names also helps with the 'which template to override?' question.
